quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 revenue was $2.9 billion, up 56% year over year, with same-store revenue up 51%; electrical segment revenue grew 88% and mechanical 47%, both benefiting from strong technology-sector demand. EPS was $10.51, more than double Q1 2025, and gross margin hit an all-time high of 26.3% (vs 22.0%). Operating income rose 132% to $486 million; EBITDA rose 116% to $524 million (trailing 12-month EBITDA $1.74 billion); free cash flow was $242 million.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 revenue $2.9 billion (+56%; same-store +51%); electrical +88%, mechanical +47%; EPS $10.51; gross margin 26.3%; EBITDA $524 million (+116%); free cash flow $242 million

quarterly_data.signal: Initial 2026 outlook: despite higher comparables in the second half, same-store revenue for full-year 2026 is expected to grow in the mid- to high-20% range; gross margins are expected to stay in the strong ranges averaged over the past several quarters. Q1 gross profit included $43 million of favorable late-stage project developments (change orders from a descope and favorable closeouts) that management called not repeatable - backing it out puts gross margin at about 25.2%. Full-year effective tax rate expected around 23%.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 same-store revenue growth mid- to high-20% range; $43 million one-time benefit; gross margin ex-benefit about 25.2%

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog ended Q1 at a record $12.5 billion, a same-store sequential increase of just over $500 million and a same-store year-over-year increase of $5.3 billion (total backlog $5 billion higher than a year ago). First-quarter bookings were especially strong in the technology sector, and advanced technology remains the largest driver of pipeline and backlog; the CEO said pipelines are still very full coast to coast while the company keeps discipline in the work it selects.
quarterly_data.figure: backlog $12.5 billion (record); same-store sequential +just over $500 million; same-store YoY +$5.3 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Revenue mix: industrial 75% of volume; advanced technology, dominated by data center work, increased to 56% of revenue; institutional 17%; commercial about 8%; construction 90% (new buildings 75%); service 10%. Modular revenue was 17% of total, and the company is on track for 4 million sq ft of modular capacity by the end of 2026 while actively evaluating additional capacity investments. The biggest epicenter of data-center demand is Texas, with the Mid-Atlantic, the Carolinas and Virginia also very active; management tracks no state data-center ban proposals affecting its geographies.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced technology (data centers) 56% of revenue; modular 17% of revenue; 4 million sq ft modular capacity by end of 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Capital expenditures were $147 million in Q1 (vs $22 million), 5.1% of revenue, including a large modular assembly building purchase in Texas (its biggest building ever, in Houston, part of getting to 4 million sq ft) that must then be fitted with cranes, robots, turntables and paint booths; similar investment is planned for the rest of the year, with full-year CapEx in the range of 5% of revenue and other building investments under review. For many of these buildings, Comfort insists that customers make multi-year commitments at volume levels as a condition of committing its capacity.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 CapEx $147 million (5.1% of revenue) vs $22 million; full-year CapEx in the range of 5% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: The CFO said growth is limited by supply, not demand: 'it's a supply issue. There is plenty more work we could take if we could possibly do it.' Labor is always the pinch point; headcount is 3,000 or 4,000 people higher than in Q1 2025 (over 23,000 employees), and materials and equipment as a percentage of revenue is up by 200 basis points. The COO added that 'the demand for data still exceeds the supply.'
quarterly_data.figure: headcount 3,000 or 4,000 higher YoY; over 23,000 employees

quarterly_data.signal: In March the company signed a definitive agreement to acquire another electrical contractor in the West (in a market where it already has a mechanical company), expected to close in early May and to initially contribute annualized revenues of roughly $250 million with EBITDA margins in the 8%-10% range. The quarterly dividend was raised to $0.80.
quarterly_data.figure: acquisition: roughly $250 million annualized revenue, EBITDA margins 8%-10%
